u1s2: Pinnipeds (pronounced ), commonly known as seals, are a widely distributed and diverse clade of carnivorous, fin-footed, semiaquatic, mostly marine mammals.
u2s2: They comprise the extant families Odobenidae (whose only living member is the walrus), Otariidae (the eared seals: sea lions and fur seals), and Phocidae (the earless seals, or true seals), with 34 extant species and more than 50 extinct species described from fossils.
u3s2: While seals were historically thought to have descended from two ancestral lines, molecular evidence supports them as a monophyletic group (descended from one ancestor).
u4s2: Seals range in size from the 1 m (3 ft 3 in) and 45 kg (100 lb) Baikal seal to the 5 m (16 ft) and 3,200 kg (7,100 lb) southern elephant seal.
u5s2: Though not as fast in the water as dolphins, seals are more flexible and agile.
u6s2: Seals mainly live in marine environments but can also be found in fresh water.
u7s2: They feed largely on fish and marine invertebrates; a few, such as the leopard seal, feed on large vertebrates, such as penguins and other seals.
u8s2: Seals produce a number of vocalizations, notably the barks of California sea lions, the gong-like calls of walruses and the complex songs of Weddell seals.
u9s2: Seals have been depicted in various cultures worldwide.
u10s2: Once relentlessly hunted by commercial industries for their products, seals are now protected by international law.
u11s2: The Japanese sea lion and the Caribbean monk seal have become extinct in the past century, while the Mediterranean monk seal and Hawaiian monk seal are ranked as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
u12s2: The common name "seal" originates from the Old English word seolh, which is in turn derived from the Proto-Germanic *selkhaz.
u13s2: American zoologist Joel Asaph Allen reviewed the world's pinnipeds in an 1880 monograph, History of North American pinnipeds, a monograph of the walruses, sea-lions, sea-bears and seals of North America.
u14s2: In 1989, Annalisa Berta and colleagues proposed the unranked clade Pinnipedimorpha to contain the fossil genus Enaliarctos and modern seals as a sister group.
u15s2: Otariids are also known as eared seals due to their pinnae.
u16s2: Otariids consist of two types: sea lions and fur seals; the latter typically being smaller, with pointier snouts, longer fore-flippers and heavier fur coats.
u17s2: Five genera and seven species (one now extinct) of sea lion are known to exist, while two genera and nine species of fur seal exist.
u18s2: While sea lions and fur seals have historically been considered separate subfamilies (Otariinae and Arctocephalinae respectively), genetic and molecular evidence has refuted this, indicating that the northern fur seal is basal to other otariids and the Australian sea lion and New Zealand sea lion are more closely related to Arctocephalus than to other sea lions.
u19s2: This animal is noticeable from its larger size (exceeded only by the elephant seals), nearly hairless skin, flattened snout and long upper canines, known as tusks.
u20s2: Phocids are known as true or "earless" seals.
u21s2: In water, true seals rely on the side-to-side motion of their hind-flippers and lower body to move forward.
u22s2: A 2006 molecular study supports the division of phocids into two monophyletic subfamilies: Monachinae, which consists of elephant seals, monk seals and Antarctic seals; and Phocinae, which consists of all the rest.
u23s2: The braincase of Potamotherium shows evidence that it used its whiskers to hunt, like modern seals.
u24s2: Both Puijila and Potamotherium fossils have been found in lake deposits, suggesting that seal ancestors were originally adapted for fresh water.
u25s2: As in modern seals, the maxilla or upper jaw bone of Pteroarctos intersects with the orbital wall.
u26s2: Seals are unique among carnivorans in that their orbital walls are mostly shaped by the maxilla and are not contained by certain facial bones.
u27s2: Pinnipeds range in size from the 1 m (3 ft 3 in) and 45 kg (100 lb) Baikal seal to the 5 m (16 ft) and 3,200 kg (7,100 lb) southern elephant seal.
u28s2: Several species have male-biased sexual dimorphism that depends on how polygynous a species is: highly polygynous species like elephant seals are extremely sexually dimorphic, while less polygynous species have males and females that are closer in size, or, in the case of Antarctic seals, females are moderately bigger.
u29s2: Fur seals have lush coats consisting of an undercoat and guard hairs.
u30s2: The pure white fur of harp seal pups conceals them in their Arctic environment.
u31s2: Seals have a layer of subcutaneous fat, known as blubber, that is particularly thick in phocids and walruses.
u32s2: Small intestine lengths range from 8 times (California sea lion) to 25 times (elephant seal) the body length.
u33s2: An appendix is absent in seals.
u34s2: Seals are more agile and flexible, and some otariids, such as the California sea lion, can make dorsal turns as the back of their heads can touch their hind flippers.
u35s2: A seal's eye is suited for seeing both underwater and in air.
u36s2: A contracted pupil is typically pear-shaped, although the bearded seal's is more horizontal.
u37s2: Compared to deep-diving elephant seals, the iris of shallower species, such as harbor seals and California sea lions, does not change much in size between constriction and dilation.
u38s2: Seals are able to see in relative darkness with a tapetum lucidum, a reflecting layer that increases sensitivity by reflecting light back through the rods.
u39s2: Polar living seals like the harp seal have corneas that can withstand the bright light that reflects off snow and ice, which would otherwise cause snow blindness.
u40s2: Flexible eye movement has been documented in seals.
u41s2: The seal eye is durable as the corneal epithelium is hardened by keratin, and the sclera is thick enough to withstand the pressures of diving.
u42s2: Seals also secrete mucus from the lacrimal gland to protect their eyes.
u43s2: One study of three species—the harbor seal, California sea lion and northern elephant seal—found that the sea lion was best adapted for airborne hearing, the elephant seal for underwater hearing and the harbor seal was equally adapted for both.
u44s2: The whiskers of some otariids grow quite long—those of the Antarctic fur seal can reach 41 cm (16 in)– while walruses have the most vibrissae, at 600–700 individual hairs.
u45s2: Harbor seals can follow hydrodynamic paths made minutes earlier, similar to a dog following a scent trail, and can even discriminate the size and type of object responsible for the trail.
u46s2: Whiskers may also play a role in navigation; spotted seals appear to use them to detect breathing holes in the ice.
u47s2: The heart of a seal is moderately flattened to allow the lungs to deflate.
u48s2: In addition, seals can tolerate large amounts of lactic acid, which reduces skeletal muscle fatigue during intense physical activity.
u49s2: Deep-diving species such as elephant seals have blood volumes that represent up to 20% of their body weight.
u50s2: While blubber and fur keep the seal warm in water, they can also overheat the animal when it is on land.
u51s2: Monk seals may even dig up the cooler layers.
u52s2: The northern fur seal cools off by panting.
u53s2: Scientists have recorded elephant seals sleeping for minutes at a time while slowly drifting downward in a belly-up orientation.
u54s2: Like other marine mammals, seals sleep in water with half of their brain awake so that they can detect and escape from predators, as well as surface for air without fully waking.
u55s2: By contrast, the consistently warm Indomalayan waters have no seals.
u56s2: Seals usually require cool, nutrient-rich waters with temperatures lower than 20 °C (68 °F).
u57s2: Only monk seals live in waters that generally lack these features.
u58s2: The Caspian seal and Baikal seal are found in large landlocked bodies of water (the Caspian Sea and Lake Baikal respectively).
u59s2: The Baikal seal is the only exclusively freshwater species.
u60s2: In polar regions, seals haul out on to both fast ice and drift ice.
u61s2: Elephant seals are at sea for most of the year and there are vast distances between their breeding and molting sites.
u62s2: The northern elephant seal is one of farthest mammalian migraters, traveling 18,000–21,000 km (11,000–13,000 mi).
u63s2: Traveling seals may reach their destination using geomagnetic fields, water and wind currents, solar and lunar positions and the temperature and chemical makeup of the water.
u64s2: When foraging, for example, the Weddell seal typically dives for no more than 15 minutes and 400 m (1,300 ft) deep, but can dive for as long as 73 minutes and reach 600 m (2,000 ft) deep.
u65s2: Northern elephant seals often dive 350–650 m (1,100–2,100 ft) for as long as 20 minutes.
u66s2: Examples are krill-eating crabeater seals, crustacean-eating ringed seals, squid specialists like the Ross seal and southern elephant seal, and the bearded seal and walrus, which specialize on benthic invertebrates.
u67s2: An exception to this is the northern elephant seal, which hunts deep in the open ocean for fish.
u68s2: The leopard seal, a prolific predator of penguins, is known to violently shake its prey to death.
u69s2: Complex serrations in the teeth of filter-feeding species, such as crabeater seals, allow water to leak out as they swallow their planktonic food.
u70s2: To subdue and kill seals, orcas strike them with their heads or tails—the latter causing them to fly in the air—or simply bite into them and rip them apart.
u71s2: Injured seals that escape are usually able to recover from their wounds.
u72s2: The polar bear is a major predator of Arctic seals and walruses, particularly pups.
u73s2: Bears may seek out seals, or simply wait for them to come by.
u74s2: Cape fur seals will even mob white sharks.
u75s2: When out at sea, northern elephant seals dive out of the reach of surface-hunting orcas and white sharks.
u76s2: The leopard seal is known to prey on many other species, especially the crabeater seal.
u77s2: Leopard seals typically target crabeater pups, particularly from November to January.
u78s2: Older crabeater seals commonly bear scars from failed leopard seal attacks; a 1977 study found that 75% of a sample of 85 individual crabeaters had these scars.
u79s2: Walruses, despite being specialized for feeding on bottom-dwelling invertebrates, occasionally prey on Arctic seals.
u80s2: Steller sea lions have been recorded eating harbor seals, northern fur seals and California sea lions, particularly pups and small adults.
u81s2: New Zealand sea lions feed on pups of some fur seal species, and the South American sea lion may prey on South American fur seals.
u82s2: These species include elephant seals, grey seals and most otariids.
u83s2: Other seals, like the walrus and most phocids, breed on ice and copulate in the water—a few land-breeding species also mate in water.
u84s2: Seals that breed on ice tend to have little or no sexual dimorphism.
u85s2: In Antarctic seals, there is some size bias in favor of females.
u86s2: Walruses and hooded seals are unique among ice-breeding species in that they have pronounced sexual dimorphism in favor of males.
u87s2: In certain species, like the Steller sea lion and northern fur seal, a dominant male can maintain a territory for as long as 2–3 months.
u88s2: Females can usually move freely between territories and males are unable to coerce females who are intent on leaving, but in some species such as the northern fur seal, South American sea lion and Australian sea lion, males keep females in their territories with threatening displays and even violence.
u89s2: In some phocid species, like the harbor seal, Weddell seal and bearded seal, the males establish "maritories" and patrol and defend the waters bordering female haul-out areas, waiting for a female to enter.
u90s2: The maritories of Weddell seal males include entries to female breathing holes in the ice.
u91s2: Lekking may also exist among California sea lions, South American fur seals, New Zealand sea lions and harbor seals.
u92s2: In some species, including elephant seals, grey seals and non-lekking walruses, males will try to lay claim to the desired females and defend them from rivals.
u93s2: Elephant seal males, in particular, establish dominance hierarchies via displays and fights, with the highest ranking males having a near monopoly on reproductive success.
u94s2: Grey seal males usually place themselves among a cluster of females whose members may change over time, while males of some walrus populations guard female herds.
u95s2: Male ringed, crabeater, spotted and hooded seals follow and defend nearby females and mate with them when they reach estrus.
u96s2: Female pinnipeds do appear to have some choice in mates, particularly in lek-breeding species like the walrus, but also in elephant seals where the males try to dominate all the females that they want to mate with.
u97s2: When a female elephant seal or grey seal is mounted by an unwanted male, she tries to resist and get away.
u98s2: Dominant female elephant seals stay in the center of the colony where they are in the domain of a more dominant male, while marginal females are left with subordinates.
u99s2: Gestation in seals (including delayed implantation) typically lasts a year.
u100s2: Phocids such as elephant seals, grey seals and hooded seals have a lactation period that lasts days or weeks, during which they fast and nurse their pups on land or ice.
u101s2: Each day until they are weaned, northern elephant seal pups gain 4 kg (9 lb).
u102s2: Alloparenting occurs in these fasting species; while most northern elephant seal mothers nurse their own pups and reject nursings from alien pups, some do accept alien pups with their own.
u103s2: For otariids and some phocids like the harbor seal, mothers fast and nurse their pups for a few days at a time.
u104s2: Lactation in otariids may last 6–11 months; in the Galápagos fur seal it can last up to three years.
u105s2: Young may wait days or weeks before entering the water; elephant seals start swimming weeks after weaning.
u106s2: While most vocals are audible to the human ear, Weddell seals have been recorded in Antarctica making ultrasonic calls underwater.
u107s2: In addition, the vocals of northern elephant seals may produce infrasonic vibrations.
u108s2: Antarctic seals are noisier on land or ice than Arctic seals due to the absence of polar bears.
u109s2: Dominant male elephant seals display their status and power with "clap-threats" and loud drum-like calls that may be modified by the proboscis.
u110s2: The Weddell seal has perhaps the most extensive vocal repertoire, producing both airborne and underwater sounds.
u111s2: When warning other seals, the calls may be pronounced by "prefixes" and "suffixes".
u112s2: The underwater vocals of Weddell seals can last 70 seconds, which is long for a marine mammal call.
u113s2: Similar calls have been recorded in other Antarctic seals and in bearded seals.
u114s2: Female seals emit a "pulsed, bawling" contact call, while pups respond by squawking.
u115s2: Other vocalizations produced by seals include grunts, rasps, rattles, creaks, warbles, clicks and whistles.
u116s2: Nevertheless, when they feel threatened, hauled-out harbor seals and Baikal seals may slap themselves with their flippers to create a warning sound.
u117s2: Visual displays also occur: Ross seals resting on the ice will show the stripes on their chests and bare their teeth to a perceived threat, while swimming Weddell seals will make an S-shaped posture to intimidate rivals under the ice.
u118s2: Male hooded seals use their inflatable nasal membranes to display to and attract females.
u119s2: === Intelligence === In a match-to-sample task study, a single California sea lion was able to demonstrate an understanding of symmetry, transitivity and equivalence; a second seal was unable to complete the tasks.
u120s2: Harbor seals have been found to adapt quickly when presented with changes to stimuli in regards to rewards and non-rewards.
u121s2: Adult male elephant seals can recognize each other's vocalizations by remembering the rhythm and timbre.
u122s2: In the 1970s, a captive harbor seal named Hoover was trained to imitate human speech and laughter.
u123s2: In Homer's Odyssey, the sea god Proteus shepherds a colony of seals.
u124s2: In northern Scotland, Celts of Orkney and the Hebrides believed in selkies—seals that could change into humans and walk on land.
u125s2: In Inuit mythology, they are associated with the goddess Sedna, who sometimes transformed into a seal.
u126s2: It was believed that marine mammals, including seals, came from her severed fingers.
u127s2: Seals have been kept in captivity since at least ancient Rome and their trainability was noticed by Pliny the Elder.
u128s2: Zoologist Georges Cuvier noted during the 19th century that wild seals show considerable affection for humans and stated that they are second only to some monkeys among wild animals in their easy tamability.
u129s2: Francis Galton noted in his seminal work on domestication that seals were a spectacular example of an animal that would most likely never be domesticated, despite their friendliness, survivability and "desire for comfort", because they serve no practical use for humans.
u130s2: Some modern exhibits have a pool with artificial haul-out sites and a rocky background, while others have seals housed in shelters located above a pool which they can jump into.
u131s2: Other commonly kept species include the grey seal and harbor seal.
u132s2: === Hunting === Humans have hunted seals since the Stone Age.
u133s2: Originally, seals were merely hit with clubs during haul-out.
u134s2: The use of firearms in seal hunting during the modern era drastically increased the number of killings.
u135s2: The skins of fur seals and phocids are made into coats, and the tusks of walruses have been used as ivory.
u136s2: There is a distinction made between the subsistence hunting of seals by indigenous peoples of the Arctic and commercial hunting: subsistence hunters depend on seal products for survival.
u137s2: However indigenous people have recently used more modern technology and are profiting more from seal products in the marketplace.
u138s2: More than 100,000 phocids (especially ringed seals) as well as around 10,000 walruses are harvested annually by native hunters.
u139s2: Harvested species included harp seals, hooded seals, Caspian seals, elephant seals, walruses and all species of fur seal.
u140s2: After the 1960s, the harvesting of seals decreased substantially as an industry after the Canadian government implemented measures to protect female seals and restrict the hunting season.
u141s2: Several species that were commercially exploited have rebounded in numbers; for example, Antarctic fur seals may have reached their pre-harvesting numbers.
u142s2: The northern elephant seal nearly went extinct in the late 19th century, with only a small population remaining on Guadalupe Island.
u143s2: Conversely, the Mediterranean monk seal was extirpated from much of the Mediterranean and its current range is still limited.
u144s2: The Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals protects species within the Antarctic and surrounding waters, but allows restricted hunting of crabeater seals, leopard seals and Weddell seals.
u145s2: Weddell seal hunting is forbidden between September and February if the animal is older than a year, to ensure healthy population growth.
u146s2: The Government of Canada permits the hunting of harp seals.
u147s2: Proponents of seal hunts insist that the animals are killed humanely and the white-coated pups are not taken, while opponents argue that it is irresponsible to kill harp seals as they are already threatened by declining habitat.
u148s2: The Caribbean monk seal has been killed and exploited by European settlers and their descendants since 1494, starting with Christopher Columbus himself.
u149s2: The seals were easy targets for organized sealers, fishermen, turtle hunters and buccaneers because they evolved with little pressure from terrestrial predators and were thus "genetically tame".
u150s2: In the Bahamas, as many as 100 seals were slaughtered in one night.
u151s2: Seal killings continued, and the last reliable report of the animal alive was in 1952 at Serranilla Bank.
u152s2: With the Japanese sea lion and the Caribbean monk seal recently extinct, ten more are considered at risk.
u153s2: They are ranked as: "Endangered": Hawaiian monk seal, Mediterranean monk seal, Galápagos fur seal, Australian sea lion, New Zealand sea lion, Caspian seal, and Galápagos sea lion.
u154s2: "Vulnerable": northern fur seal, hooded seal, and walrus. Pinnipeds face various threats.
u155s2: Gillnetting and seine netting is a significant cause of mortality in seals and other marine mammals.
u156s2: Species commonly entangled include California sea lions, Hawaiian monk seals, northern fur seals and Cape fur seals.
u157s2: In 2010 and 2011, sea ice in the Northwest Atlantic was at or near an all-time low and harp seals as well as ringed seals that bred on thin ice saw increased death rates.
u158s2: In the Antarctic, the decreased duration and extent of the sea ice and nutrient availability could potentially reduce the survival of Weddell seal pups and may have important implications for population growth rates.
u159s2: Antarctic fur seals in South Georgia in the South Atlantic saw major decreases over a 20-year study, during which scientists measured increased sea surface temperature anomalies.
u160s2: Seals also conflict with fisheries; a 2024 metastudy found that globally pinnipeds affected over 33 percent of fishing days and stole over 13 percent of catches.
u161s2: In the 1980s and 1990s, South African politicians and fishermen demanded that brown fur seals be culled, believing that the animals competed with commercial fisheries.
u162s2: Scientific studies found that culling fur seals would actually have a negative effect on the fishing industry, and the culling option was dropped in 1993.
